summary:
An interactive platform was developed that brings together climate records for Chile over the last 25 years (2000–2024). To build it, we used data from NASA satellites and from Chilean government agencies.

The challenge we selected was Earth System Trend Detective. Our platform lets users explore the NASA data for this period by choosing among the variables (rainfall, snow, humidity and heat), or by browsing the data without selecting any. Users can also learn how to be a climate detective and play at being one.

F.O.C.O. is a viewer that allows students, teachers and citizens to see how Chile’s climate has changed, to learn about the data and to use it. It also helps people recognize the impact of climate variables on the country’s natural zones and regions, at a time when misinformation has been growing.
details:
FOCO is an interactive web page that lets anyone see how Chile’s climate has changed between 2000 and 2024. Many people hear about climate change but cannot see it in their own region, and the data that could show them is hard to read. We built FOCO to close that gap, so that young people, families and decision-makers can explore it without technical training.

The page works like a detective investigation. Users pick a variable, such as rainfall or humidity, then a place: all of Chile, one of five macrozones or one of sixteen regions. They also choose a time range. FOCO then draws maps, color strips and trend charts from 25 years of monthly NASA satellite and model data. Each trend carries an arrow: a strong color means the change is unlikely to be chance, while “=” means there is no clear trend. A combined variable merges several signals into one picture of how dry or wet a place is becoming. Two mascots, Foquito and Novatina, answer questions in a chat, and the whole page works in Spanish and English.

We considered scientific honesty and our audience at every step. We used long data series, kept “no clear trend” visible and warned users that one year is not a trend. We also used plain language, a glossary and a responsive layout that works on phones.

The project is creative because it turns statistics into a story, with clues, mascots and a game instead of a plain dashboard. It is also easy to share: it is a single lightweight page, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Python for data processing and Playwright for testing. It runs on standard laptops, is published on nuevofoco.org and can be opened with a QR code.

Our intended impact is that people understand the climate of their own region, learn to question data and join better-informed conversations about water and drought.
